title: Causative: have/get something done
tagline: You didn't do it yourself — you arranged it, ordered it, or it just happened to you.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze (had / to / done)
Speaking Part 1 — talking about everyday services and arrangements
why: Not every action in English needs the person who does it as the subject. When you pay someone to cut your hair, ask a friend to lend you a charger, or your phone gets stolen on the bus, the causative structures let you say all of that without naming who actually did the action. B2 First tests the exact pattern for each one — and they are not interchangeable.

diagrams.title: have / get something done
diagrams.caption: Someone else does the action for you — you only arrange or pay for it.

diagrams.title: Three ways to involve other people

rows.label: Example
cells: I'll have Liam bring the chairs.
She got her dad to drive us.

branches.label: make (+ sb + infinitive) — force
items: The teacher made us redo the exercise.

branches.label: let (+ sb + infinitive) — permit, informal
items: My parents let me stay out later.

branches.label: allow (+ sb + to-infinitive) — permit, formal
items: Students are allowed to leave early on Fridays.
The school doesn't allow phones in class.

branches.label: have / get sth done — arrange a service
items: I need to get my laptop fixed.

branches.label: have sth happen to you — misfortune
items: He had his wallet stolen at the fair.
She had her essay marked down for late submission.

head: Pattern
Structure
Example
rows: We have the equipment checked every term.
They had the hall decorated for the ceremony.
I need to get my phone screen fixed.
I'll have my essay proofread before Friday.
Miss Vega had Nadia read the announcement.
He got his sister to help with the poster.
The coach made the team run an extra lap.
Liam had his charger stolen during the trip.

use.point: have/get something done: arranging for someone else to do a job for you

examples.text: We had the science posters printed at the shop near school.
examples.note: a service arranged, not done by hand

examples.text: Sofia is getting her bike fixed before the weekend trip.
examples.note: get = a more informal alternative to have

examples.text: The club will have the new kit delivered by next month.

use.point: have/get somebody do something: asking or persuading someone directly

examples.text: Miss Vega had Mateo explain the rules to the new students.
Nadia got her older brother to lend her his calculator.
I'll have Liam set up the projector before the presentation.

use.point: make, let and allow: obligation and permission

examples.text: The coach made the whole team arrive an hour early for training.
examples.note: make + bare infinitive = force, no choice

examples.text: My parents finally let me go to the concert on my own.
The school doesn't allow students to use phones during exams.

use.point: have something happen to you: things that happen to you, often unfortunate

examples.text: Sofia had her essay marked down for handing it in late.
We had our tent blown away during the storm on the trip.
examples.note: an event, not something you arranged

watch_out.wrong: I got him fix the printer.
watch_out.right: I got him to fix the printer.
watch_out.why: After get + person, the infinitive always needs to.

watch_out.wrong: The teacher had us to hand in our phones.
watch_out.right: The teacher had us hand in our phones.
watch_out.why: After have + person, use the bare infinitive, with no to.

watch_out.wrong: They didn't let us to leave the building.
watch_out.right: They didn't let us leave the building.
watch_out.why: Let is always followed by the bare infinitive, never to.

watch_out.wrong: The school doesn't allow students use their phones.
watch_out.right: The school doesn't allow students to use their phones.

watch_out.wrong: We were made redo the whole project.
watch_out.right: We were made to redo the whole project.
watch_out.why: In the passive, make takes to before the infinitive, even though the active form doesn't.

watch_out.wrong: I had my hair cutted yesterday.
watch_out.why: Cut is an irregular verb — the past participle has the same form as the base verb.

dialogue.title: Getting ready for the science fair
dialogue.context: Nadia, Mateo and Liam are organising the last details before the school science fair, and something has already gone wrong.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Did you have the posters printed in the end? The shop said Wednesday.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Yes, and I got my sister to laminate them so they survive the day.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Smart. I had my charger stolen from my bag yesterday, so I'll need to borrow one.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Seriously? Miss Vega will probably have someone bring a spare from the staff room.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: She always does. She had Sofia set up the extension leads first thing this morning.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Good, because the caretaker won't let us use the hall wiring without supervision.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Right. And remember, they don't allow us to bring food near the electronics table.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Noted. I'll have the volunteers check that before the judges arrive.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: One more thing — did you get your model repaired after it broke last week?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Yes, my uncle fixed it in an hour. Now let's just hope nobody has anything else go wrong today.

items.sentence: We ___ the hall decorated for the ceremony by the art club.
items.why: arranging a service for you → have sth done

items.sentence: Miss Vega ___ Nadia read the announcement to the class.
items.why: have + person + bare infinitive = a direct instruction

items.sentence: He finally ___ his cousin to help him with the coursework.
The coach ___ the team run three extra laps for being late.
items.why: make + bare infinitive = force, no choice

items.sentence: My parents won't ___ me stay out past ten on a school night.
Liam ___ his bike stolen outside the library last week.
items.why: something unfortunate happened to him → have sth happen

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct causative form of the verb in brackets.

items.sentence: We ___ (print) the tickets at the shop near the school.
Sofia ___ (fix) her laptop before the deadline.
The teacher ___ (redo) our whole essay because of the formatting.
Nadia ___ (lend) her a jacket by her best friend.
answers: got her best friend to lend her a jacket
had her best friend lend her a jacket

items.sentence: My parents don't ___ (use) my phone after nine o'clock.
The school doesn't ___ (bring) energy drinks onto the premises.
Mateo ___ (steal) his headphones on the bus this morning.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first. Use the word given. Do not change it. Use between two and five words.

items.first: A professional photographer took our class photo.
Nadia persuaded her brother to lend her his laptop.
The teacher forced the students to rewrite their essays.
Someone stole Sofia's scarf while she was at practice.
The school permits senior students to use the study room at lunchtime.

summary: have/get + object + past participle = you arrange for someone else to do it for you: I had my bike repaired.
have + person + bare infinitive is a direct instruction; get + person + to-infinitive involves persuading them.
make and let take the bare infinitive; allow needs to — but the passive be made to does too.
The same have + object + past participle pattern also describes something unfortunate that happened to you.
Choose the pattern by who actually performs the action: you, someone you ask, someone you pay, or nobody at all.
